title: The Platinum Rule
author: Joel Trammell
summary: Trammell argues that managers default to assuming everyone is like them, and that this blind spot is a core cause of management failure. He confesses he was in his mid-thirties before realizing not everyone wants to be a CEO. He contrasts the Silver Rule, which only avoids imposing what you would not choose, and the Golden Rule, which still rests on what the manager would want, with the Platinum Rule: treat people the way they want to be treated. The move is to turn the familiar ethical rule into a management practice that requires learning each employee's preferences. He offers concrete examples such as public recognition that delights one person and mortifies another, plus questions about work rhythm, social energy, closeness to the manager and autonomy. His practical advice is to observe, talk with the employee about what you notice, adjust, and keep running notes on each person.
points: Most managers operate on the unexamined assumption that everyone is like them, which leads them to manage clones of themselves.
The Silver and Golden Rules both anchor on the manager's own preferences; the Platinum Rule makes the employee's wants the standard.
Identical experiences, such as public recognition, produce opposite reactions in introverts and extroverts, so recognition must be tailored.
Useful probes cover best working hours, group versus solo energy, personal versus purely professional relationship, and autonomy versus guidance.
Keeping a running record of observations about each employee is the recommended tool for applying the rule.
quotes: There’s nothing malicious about it. Our preferences and personality and strengths are just so natural to us that it’s hard to imagine other people not sharing them.

There’s no correct answer to any given problem an employee is having. The answer is, almost always, it depends on who you’re managing. Your job as a manager is to learn enough to make these distinctions between people and tailor your management style accordingly.

The Golden Rule. As stated in the Christian tradition, “Do unto others as you would have them do unto you.” Applied to the workplace, this twist gives the manager more agency. It asks you to be the kind of manager you would want to have.

The Platinum Rule. The best standard for managers advises them to “treat others the way they want to be treated.” Now the manager is required to learn how each specific employee works and then empathetically meet their specific needs.

For an introverted employee, being called up to a podium to receive a plaque from the CEO in front of the entire company might be a deeply mortifying experience. But for another more outgoing employee, that plaque and the standing ovation might make his month. These two people had the exact same experience, but it caused totally different reactions in them.
For each employee, keep your own record of these observations. These running notes are an invaluable tool in applying the Platinum Rule.

Yes, some people may actually do their best work at 9:00 p.m. from their couch. As unfathomable as your employees’ working styles may seem to you, you’ll be a more effective manager once you recognize them and begin treating people as they want to be treated—not as you would want to be treated.
